content.name: p
children: The use of Mutual TLS (mTLS) authentication ensures that traffic is secure and trusted in both directions between webhook services and listeners. With mTLS, both webhook service and listener pass through a TLS handshake — in which both systems present trusted certificates — before the webhook notification is sent.

content.name: p
children: This method delivers a stronger authentication between the webhook service and listener and ensures communication confidentiality — a webhook message is sent only after both sides are authenticated. When combined with webhook signatures, it also delivers message integrity.

content.name: p
children: . Once the TLS session is terminated — commonly at a load balancer, API gateway, or CDN in front of the listener — the application only sees a plain HTTP request, plus whatever headers the proxy chooses to forward about the client certificate. That has two consequences:

children.name: li
children: The application must trust the proxy to have validated the provider's certificate, and should reject requests that didn't arrive through it.

children.name: li
children: Nothing proves the payload wasn't changed between the proxy and the application, or after it was written to a queue. A signature —
— travels with the message, so it can be verified anywhere, at any time.

content.name: p
children: For most consumers, mTLS is defense in depth on top of signatures rather than a replacement for them.

content.name: p
children: However, mTLS is often difficult to configure (when compared against HMAC). It also requires updates whenever TLS certificates are issued, renewed, or revoked both on the webhook service and the listener side. This additional burden is considered overkill for most webhook use-cases.
